clinicalPearls: A benign epithelial ovarian tumour lined by mucin-secreting, gastrointestinal-type columnar epithelium
Characteristically multiloculated and can grow very large, sometimes filling the abdomen, and is usually unilateral
Ultrasound typically shows a multilocular cyst with thin septations and mucinous fluid of varying echogenicity
Distinguished from borderline and malignant mucinous tumours by the absence of proliferation, atypia, and invasion; extensive sampling is needed because these features can be focal
Bilateral mucinous tumours should prompt a search for a gastrointestinal primary, as metastatic mucinous carcinoma can mimic a primary ovarian lesion
Rupture or spillage of mucinous contents is a concern given the association of mucinous tumours with pseudomyxoma peritonei, although most true pseudomyxoma arises from an appendiceal source
Managed by cystectomy or oophorectomy with care to avoid intraoperative rupture
reference.pathophysiology: Mucinous cystadenomas are benign surface-epithelial tumours lined by tall columnar cells containing abundant mucin, resembling endocervical or, more often, gastrointestinal epithelium. The epithelium is a single orderly layer without stratification, atypia, or stromal invasion, and copious mucin secretion generates a characteristically multiloculated cyst that can reach a very large size. Because malignant or borderline change may be focal within an otherwise benign tumour, thorough histological sampling is essential. Spillage of mucin-secreting epithelium can theoretically seed the peritoneum, but classic pseudomyxoma peritonei is now recognised to originate predominantly from a low-grade appendiceal mucinous neoplasm rather than from the ovary itself.
additionalDifferentials: Mucinous borderline tumour or mucinous carcinoma
Metastatic gastrointestinal or appendiceal mucinous tumour
Mature cystic teratoma with a mucinous component
additionalInvestigations: Transvaginal and abdominal ultrasound to demonstrate a multilocular mucinous cyst
Pelvic and abdominal cross-sectional imaging for large lesions and to assess the appendix and bowel
Tumour markers including CA125, CEA, and CA19-9 to aid stratification
Bowel evaluation when a metastatic mucinous tumour is suspected, especially if bilateral
Histology with extensive sampling to exclude borderline or malignant foci
Assessment of the appendix if pseudomyxoma or mucinous ascites is found
redFlags: Solid areas, thick irregular septations, or ascites suggesting borderline or malignant change
Bilateral mucinous tumours raising concern for metastatic gastrointestinal disease
Mucinous ascites or peritoneal deposits suggesting pseudomyxoma peritonei
Acute pain from torsion or rupture of a large cyst
reference.prognosis: Excellent for genuinely benign lesions, which are cured by complete excision; the main caveats are the need for adequate sampling to exclude malignancy and avoidance of rupture given the association of mucinous disease with peritoneal spread.
pitfalls: Inadequate sampling that misses a focal borderline or malignant component
Assuming a bilateral mucinous tumour is a primary ovarian lesion rather than a metastasis
Causing intraoperative rupture and spillage of mucinous contents
Attributing pseudomyxoma peritonei to the ovary without evaluating the appendix
references: WHO Classification of Female Genital Tumours
Blaustein's Pathology of the Female Genital Tract
management: Definitive treatment is complete surgical excision, either cystectomy or unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy
Remove the specimen intact where feasible, avoiding intraoperative rupture or spillage due to the theoretical risk of peritoneal seeding
In younger patients wanting to preserve fertility, ovarian cystectomy with preservation of the contralateral ovary and uterus is preferred when feasible
Send the specimen for extensive histologic sampling since a focal borderline or malignant component can be missed on limited sampling
If the tumour is bilateral or mucinous ascites or peritoneal disease is present, evaluate the appendix and bowel for a primary gastrointestinal or appendiceal mucinous neoplasm
Surgery alone is curative for confirmed benign disease; there is no systemic or radiotherapeutic line of therapy for this entity
Radiotherapy has no role in management

Systemic cytotoxic or targeted therapy has no role unless final histology upgrades the diagnosis to a borderline or invasive mucinous tumour, in which case management follows the pathway for that upgraded diagnosis
CA125 is not expressed by mucinous ovarian tumours and is unreliable for this histology, while CEA and CA19-9 can help preoperative stratification of an adnexal mass
Postoperative clinical and imaging follow-up is reasonable to confirm resolution and detect recurrence or a missed contralateral lesion
No ongoing surveillance regimen akin to malignancy follow-up is needed once complete excision and adequate benign histology are confirmed

Refer to gynaecologic oncology if final histology shows borderline or invasive features, the tumour is bilateral, or mucinous ascites or peritoneal disease raises concern for pseudomyxoma peritonei or a gastrointestinal primary
A general gynaecologist can manage a mass with reassuring imaging and no red-flag findings, reserving oncology referral for atypical, bilateral, or histologically upgraded cases
